mn96:3.16: In the Buddhist Sanghas of bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs, there were people from each of the four ‘castes’, and they certainly did not follow the rule prescribed by the brahmins who put themselves at the apex of society. In the Sangha, reverence was given according to seniority from the time of ordination.
mn96:4.4: The idiom ‘brāhmaṇā appaṭiññāya tesaṁ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṁ, atha ca pana...paññapenti’ is peculiar; atha ca pana here seems equivalent to ‘in that’, ‘since’, or better, ‘when’ — i.e. the brahmins prescribe this without the consent of other ascetics and brahmins.
mn96:7.7: Both these are present as views in the modern world too, for high rank, high caste (or birth), and great property are still reckoned by some to be marks of ‘superior’ people; others, equally wrongly, look down on these as evidence of inferiority. Both attitudes cause unending trouble.
mn96:10.13: Asitabyābhaṅgi—sickle and carrying-yoke: literally ‘the yoke loaded with mown harvest’; asita is from a root meaning to cut or mow, and byābhaṅgi denotes the pingo or yoke on which loads are carried.
mn96:10.16: This is also a veiled attack by the brahmin, since the Buddha came of the noble caste but did not live by its prescribed source of wealth, the bow and quiver, i.e. warfare; and he and his bhikkhus lived on alms-food, which by this scheme was the brahmins’ own source of wealth.
mn96:13.1: He abstains from all sexual activity, leading the life divine in purity. The expression ‘ārādhako hoti ñāyaṁ dhammaṁ’ (‘he has attained success in the true, wholesome Dhamma’) recurs spoken by a brahmin in Sutta 99.
